chapter.name: Materials Around Us
chapter.blurb: Materials are the substances objects are made of; grouping materials by a shared property is classification. Materials have properties -- lustre, hardness, transparency, solubility in water -- and anything with mass and volume is called matter, measured with the SI units gram/kilogram (mass) and litre/millilitre/cubic metre (volume).

scope_in.item: Any substance used to create an object is called a material; an object can be made of one material or a combination of materials, and one material can be used for more than one object

Classification: arranging objects/materials into groups based on a chosen common property (shape, colour, material, hardness, shine, etc.); the same set of objects can be classified in more than one valid way
Lustrous (shiny surface, usually metals) and non-lustrous materials; metals can lose lustre due to air/moisture; a non-metal can be made to look shiny by polishing or coating
Hard (difficult to compress/scratch) and soft (easily compressed/scratched) materials; hardness/softness is relative, e.g. rubber is harder than sponge but softer than iron

Transparent (clearly see-through), translucent (hazy/partial view) and opaque (cannot see through) materials, with examples: glass/water/cellophane (transparent), frosted glass/butter paper (translucent), wood/cardboard/metals (opaque)

Soluble (completely disappears when stirred in water) and insoluble (remains visible after stirring) materials; sugar and salt are soluble, sand and sawdust are insoluble; some liquids mix completely with water and some form a separate layer; oxygen gas dissolves in water and is important for aquatic life

Mass as the property of being heavier or lighter, measured by weighing; SI units gram (g) and kilogram (kg), with the abbreviation convention (no space in 'kg', a space between number and unit, no plural 's')
Volume as the space occupied by a material; SI-related units litre (L) and millilitre (mL) with their abbreviation convention, and cubic metre (m3) as the SI unit of volume; 1 m3 = 1000 L
Matter is defined as anything that occupies space (has volume) and has mass; materials are types of matter

concepts.name: Materials and objects; classification by a common property
concepts.description: A material is any substance used to create an object; classification is grouping objects or materials by a chosen common property.
concepts.idea: A material is any substance used to create an object; an object can be made of one or several materials, and the same material can be used for many different objects.
concepts.rule: To classify means to arrange objects or materials into groups based on a chosen common property such as shape, colour, material or texture; the same set of items can be grouped in more than one valid way depending on which property is chosen.
concepts.example: A pen can be made of plastic, metal and ink together, while both a plastic bucket and a plastic toy share the same material despite being different objects.

concepts.name: Appearance of materials: lustrous and non-lustrous
concepts.description: Materials with a shiny surface (usually metals) are lustrous; those without are non-lustrous, and shine can sometimes be faked by a coating.
concepts.idea: Materials that have a shiny surface show lustre and are called lustrous; those without a shiny surface are non-lustrous.
concepts.rule: Most lustrous materials are metals, but metals can lose lustre due to air and moisture; not everything shiny is a metal, since a surface can be made to look shiny by polishing or a coating.
concepts.example: A freshly cut piece of aluminium foil is shiny and lustrous, while paper, wood, rubber and jute are non-lustrous; a wax-coated surface can look lustrous without being a metal.

concepts.name: Hardness of materials: hard and soft
concepts.description: Materials that resist compressing or scratching are hard; those that compress or scratch easily are soft, and hardness is always relative.
concepts.idea: Materials that are difficult to compress or scratch are called hard; those that can be compressed or scratched easily are soft.
concepts.rule: Hardness and softness are relative -- a material is judged harder or softer only by comparison with another material, for example rubber is harder than sponge but softer than iron.
concepts.example: A metal key scratches wood, chalk or a candle easily, showing the key is harder, while pressing an eraser or sponge compresses it easily, showing it is soft.

concepts.name: Transparency of materials: transparent, translucent and opaque
concepts.description: Materials are grouped by how clearly you can see through them: transparent (clearly), translucent (hazily) or opaque (not at all).
concepts.idea: Materials through which objects can be seen clearly are transparent; those through which nothing can be seen are opaque; those through which objects can be seen but not clearly are translucent.
concepts.rule: These three categories describe how see-through a material is: fully clear (transparent), partially clear or hazy (translucent), or not see-through at all (opaque).
concepts.example: Glass and water are transparent, wood and metals are opaque, and frosted glass or butter paper are translucent.

concepts.name: Solubility of materials in water: soluble and insoluble
concepts.description: A material that completely dissolves when stirred in water is soluble; one that stays visible is insoluble, and this applies to solids, liquids and gases.
concepts.idea: A material that completely disappears when mixed and stirred in water is soluble; a material that does not disappear even after stirring is insoluble.
concepts.rule: Solubility applies to solids, liquids and gases -- some liquids mix completely with water while others separate into a layer, and gases like oxygen dissolve in water.
concepts.example: Sugar and salt dissolve completely in water, while sand and sawdust do not disappear even after stirring; oxygen gas dissolves in water and is needed by fish.

questions.q: Explain how you would find out whether a spoonful of a new white powder is soluble or insoluble in water.
questions.a: Add the powder to a glass of water and stir well for a few minutes; if the powder completely disappears, it is soluble; if some or all of it remains visible even after stirring for a while, it is insoluble.
s: Describes mixing and stirring the powder in water
States the correct criterion for soluble vs insoluble

questions.q: ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) is prepared by mixing sugar and salt in water. This works because sugar and salt are
questions.a: soluble in water

questions.q: A glass of water with sand stirred into it is left standing for an hour. What will most likely happen?
questions.a: The sand will settle at the bottom since it is insoluble
o: The sand will settle at the bottom since it is insoluble
The water will turn into sand
The sand will float on top and dissolve slowly

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to test and compare the solubility of sugar, sand and chalk powder in water, and predict your results.
questions.a: Sample: Take three glasses of water, add a teaspoon of sugar to the first, sand to the second, and chalk powder to the third; stir each well and observe. Predicted result: sugar disappears completely, while sand and chalk powder remain visible and settle at the bottom.
s: Describes a fair, comparable test for all three materials
States a clear observation criterion
Gives a correct predicted result for all three materials

questions.q: A student stirs salt into water and it disappears; the same student stirs sand into water and it settles at the bottom. What can be concluded?
questions.a: Salt is soluble in water while sand is insoluble
o: Salt is soluble in water while sand is insoluble
Sand is more soluble than salt

questions.q: Consider: (I) All solids dissolve completely if you stir them in water for long enough. (II) Some liquids do not mix with water and form a separate layer. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only II

questions.q: Explain why it is not correct to say that insoluble materials disappear slowly, just more slowly than soluble ones.
questions.a: This is incorrect because insoluble materials do not disappear at all, even after being stirred for a long time -- for example, sand and sawdust remain visible in water no matter how long you stir; only soluble materials like sugar and salt actually disappear by dissolving.
s: Explains that insoluble materials do not disappear at all, not just slowly
Supports with a correct example

questions.q: A shopkeeper says a powder is '90% soluble' in water. Based on what you have learned, where solubility is described simply as soluble or insoluble, do you think this claim makes complete sense? Justify your answer.
questions.a: The chapter only describes solubility as a simple soluble/insoluble split, so a claim like '90% soluble' goes beyond what this chapter defines; it would need extra explanation to be properly understood at this level.
s: Notes that the chapter's idea of solubility is a simple soluble/insoluble split
States the claim needs further explanation to be understood at this level
Reasoning is coherent and related to the chapter's content

questions.q: Invent a fun classroom game to help classmates remember which of five materials -- sugar, salt, sand, chalk powder, sawdust -- are soluble and which are insoluble in water. Describe the game and how points are scored.
questions.a: Sample: 'Dissolve or Not' game -- call out one material at a time; students who think it is soluble raise a blue card, and those who think it is insoluble raise a red card; award a point for each correct guess (sugar and salt are soluble; sand, chalk powder and sawdust are insoluble). The student with the most points wins.
s: Describes a workable game mechanic
Correctly identifies which materials are soluble/insoluble in the scoring
Explains how points/winning are determined

concepts.name: Mass, volume and matter; SI units
concepts.description: Anything with mass and volume is matter; mass is measured in grams/kilograms and volume in litres/millilitres/cubic metres.
concepts.idea: Anything that occupies space and has mass is called matter; mass is the quantity of matter (measured in grams/kilograms) and volume is the space occupied by matter (measured in litres/millilitres, with cubic metre as the SI unit).
concepts.rule: All materials are matter because they have both mass and volume; SI abbreviation conventions: kg (no space, no plural), L uppercase, mL lowercase-m-uppercase-L, and 1 m3 = 1000 L.
concepts.example: A glass tumbler half-filled with water has less volume of water than one nearly full, even though both tumblers have the same capacity; weighing two paper cups on a balance compares their mass.

questions.a: matter

questions.q: Which of these correctly follows the SI abbreviation rules described in the chapter?
Two paper cups are filled halfway, one with sand and one with pebbles. Explain how you would use a balance to find out which one has more mass.
questions.a: Place each filled cup on one side of the balance in turn, or one on each side together, and compare which side goes down; the cup that makes the balance dip down has more mass.

questions.a: because mass is often determined by weighing an object
o: because mass is often determined by weighing an object
because weight and mass are exactly the same idea at this level
because weight has no connection to mass

questions.q: A shopkeeper says a bag of rice has a mass of 5 kgs. What is wrong with this, based on the chapter's rule?
questions.a: The correct abbreviation is '5 kg', not '5 kgs', since kg does not take a plural s
o: The correct abbreviation is '5 kg', not '5 kgs', since kg does not take a plural s
5 kg cannot be a valid mass
kg should be written as Kg

questions.q: You are given a bottle labelled '1 L' and asked to explain to a younger student what this tells us about the bottle's contents. Using the ideas of matter, mass and volume, write your explanation.
questions.a: The label '1 L' tells us the volume of liquid the bottle holds, the amount of space the liquid inside occupies; since the liquid has both mass and takes up space, it is matter, and litre is the unit used to measure how much space it occupies, unlike kilograms, which would measure its mass instead.
s: Correctly explains that 1 L states the liquid's volume
Connects this to the liquid being matter
Correctly distinguishes volume units from mass units

questions.q: A cup of sand and a cup of pebbles have the same volume but different masses when weighed. What does this tell you?
questions.a: The two materials can have the same volume yet different mass, since mass and volume are independent properties
o: The two materials can have the same volume yet different mass, since mass and volume are independent properties
The two materials must be identical
Only one of them is matter

questions.q: Assertion (A): Air is not matter, since it has no mass and cannot be weighed. Reason (R): Anything that occupies space and has mass is called matter. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Explain why having mass alone, without also occupying space, would not be enough to call something matter, based on how the chapter defines matter.
questions.a: The chapter defines matter as anything that BOTH occupies space AND has mass; if something only had mass but occupied no space at all, it would not fit the chapter's definition of matter, since both properties are required together.
s: Correctly states matter needs both properties
Explains that having only one property would not be enough by this definition

questions.q: A classmate claims, 'Since I cannot see air, it cannot be matter.' Do you agree with this reasoning? Justify your answer using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: No, I disagree. Whether something can be seen is a completely different property from whether it is matter; matter is defined only by occupying space and having mass, and air does both, even though air is transparent and hard to see.
s: Disagrees with the claim
Explains that visibility/transparency is unrelated to being matter
Correctly argues air has volume and mass, so it is matter

questions.q: Design a simple demonstration to show a younger student that air is matter, using only ordinary classroom objects. Describe your demonstration and what result would prove your point.
questions.a: Sample: Inflate a balloon and let the air out into an empty, closed plastic bottle underwater, showing bubbles rise, to show air takes up space. To show air has mass, carefully weigh a fully inflated balloon against the same balloon after letting the air out; the inflated balloon should weigh very slightly more.
s: Describes a workable demonstration showing air occupies space
Describes or extends the demonstration to also address air having mass
States a clear expected result that supports air being matter
